options.misconception: Confuses the stated justification with the motive Las Casas names.
options.text: A sincere desire to spread Christianity.

options.misconception: Blames the king for what Las Casas blames on the colonists.
options.text: Direct orders from the Spanish king to destroy Native communities.

options.misconception: Invents attacks the passage says never happened.

options.text: Gold, and the ambition and greed for quick wealth and status.

rationales.A: Las Casas names gold and greed as the motive, not missionary zeal. Christianity was the stated justification, not the driving force he describes.
rationales.B: He blames the colonists' avarice, not royal orders. The Crown later passed the reforming New Laws, which cut against this claim.
rationales.C: The passage names ambition and greed for gold as the motive, not Native attacks. Nothing in the excerpt describes self-defense; the destruction it describes is unprovoked cruelty driven by avarice.
rationales.D: Las Casas is explicit: the colonists wanted gold, quick wealth, and the status it bought. Ambition and avarice are the motives he names.
rationales.general:
1. Let the author name the crime. Las Casas opens with one word for the cause: ambition and avarice, plus the vast wealth of the region.
2. Check the other motives against the text. He says nothing about missionary zeal or royal orders driving the destruction.
3. Note what he rules out. Nothing in the excerpt describes self-defense; the destruction it describes is unprovoked cruelty driven by avarice.
4. Match the motive to the key. Gold and greed for quick wealth and status is what he describes.
Remember: when a source names a motive in its own words, use the author's words, not the motive you expect.

stimulus.source_note: Bartolome de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written 1542, published 1552; this English translation, 1689). Text verbatim from Project Gutenberg EBook #20321. Archaic spelling kept.
stimulus.text: Finally, in one word, their Ambition and Avarice, than which the heart of Man never entertained greater, and the vast Wealth of those Regions; the Humility and Patience of the Inhabitants (which made their approach to these Lands more facil and easie) did much promote the business: Whom they so despicably contemned, that they treated them (I speak of things which I was an Eye Witness of, without the least fallacy) not as Beasts, which I cordially wished they would, but as the most abject dung and filth of the Earth.
